source_refs.note: Exercise 14.4 Q4 (i)-(ii), book p.290 (PDF 295). Answer key PDF 312: (i) 5/2, (ii) +-1, both correct (sympy). Solution book PDF 1272-1274 agrees.

blocks.prompt: 4 (i) Find the constant \(\alpha\) such that the vectors are coplanar: \(\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\) and \(3\underline{i} - \alpha \underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
An unknown-constant question with a coplanarity condition.
We must find \(\alpha\).
Plan: set the scalar triple product (a determinant containing \(\alpha\)) equal to 0 and solve.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - 3\underline{k}\), \(3\underline{i} - \alpha\underline{j} + 5\underline{k}\) are coplanar.
To find: \(\alpha\).
Method: coplanar \(\Leftrightarrow\) scalar triple product \(= 0\) (14.4.5).

Write the determinant
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & -3 \\ 3 & -\alpha & 5 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: One row per vector; \(\alpha\) is treated like a number.

Set equal to 0 and solve
\[10 - 4\alpha = 0\]
\[\alpha = \dfrac{10}{4} = \dfrac{5}{2}\]
Why: Coplanar vectors have triple product 0.

Check
\[-10 - \tfrac{15}{2} + 14 - \tfrac{5}{2} + 6 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Putting \(\alpha = \frac{5}{2}\) back into the unsimplified expansion gives 0.

blocks.prompt: 4 (ii) Find the constant \(\alpha\) such that the vectors are coplanar: \(\underline{i} - 2\alpha \underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\) and \(\alpha \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + \underline{k}\).
blocks.explanation:
Same type as part (i), but \(\alpha\) now appears in two vectors.
We must find every value of \(\alpha\).
Plan: expand the determinant; it gives a quadratic in \(\alpha\); set it to 0.
steps:
Given: \(\underline{i} - 2\alpha\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\), \(\alpha\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + \underline{k}\) are coplanar.
To find: \(\alpha\).
Method: scalar triple product \(= 0\).

Write the determinant
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -2\alpha & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ \alpha & -2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: One row per vector.

Expand along row 1
\[= 1(-2 + 4) + 2\alpha(1 - 2\alpha) - 1(-2 + 2\alpha)\]
\[= 2 + 2\alpha - 4\alpha^2 + 2 - 2\alpha\]
\[= 4 - 4\alpha^2\]
Why: Minors \((-2)(1) - (2)(-2) = 2\), \((1)(1) - (2)(\alpha) = 1 - 2\alpha\), \((1)(-2) - (-2)(\alpha) = -2 + 2\alpha\); the middle entry \(-2\alpha\) with sign \(-\) gives \(+2\alpha\).

Solve
\[4 - 4\alpha^2 = 0\]
\[\alpha^2 = 1\]
\[\alpha = \pm 1\]
Why: Both square roots satisfy the equation.

Check
\[\alpha = 1:\ \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} - \underline{k},\ \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + 2\underline{k},\ \underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + \underline{k}\]
\[\alpha = -1:\ \alpha\underline{i} - 2\underline{j} + \underline{k} = -(\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k})\]
Why: For \(\alpha = 1\) every vector has \(y\)-component \(= -2 \times\) its \(x\)-component, so all lie in the plane \(y = -2x\). For \(\alpha = -1\) the third vector is minus the first, so they are parallel and the three are coplanar.
